newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BAYERN TAKE ON DORTMUND'S PRETENDERS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-BAYERN TAKE ON DORTMUND'S PRETENDERS.

text.p: The German soccer hierarchy may have changed over the past quarter of a century but the main attraction still looks the same -- Bayern v Borussia.

In Germany's golden era in the 1970s, the match of the season was always Bayern Munich against Borussia Moenchengladbach when the country's leading players came face-to-face in often dramatic encounters.
The corresponding clash of the 1990s is Bayern v Borussia Dortmund, the Bundesliga's model club of the modern era who have beaten the Bavarians to the title for the last two seasons.
Even when Dortmund are struggling with an array of injuries, Sunday evening's clash in Munich's Olympic stadium is sure to be a sell-out. Millions more will watch the game live on television.

For the big names of the 1970s like Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Mueller, Berti Vogts and Guenter Netzer read World Cup and Euro 96 stars like Juergen Klinsmann, Lothar Matthaeus, Matthias Sammer and Andy Moeller.
In the 1970s most of the German national team which won the 1974 World Cup came from Moenchengladbach and Bayern who dominated the Bundesliga during most of the decade.
Their clashes are still shown on television 20 years later. But the Borussia half of German football's powerbase has changed.
Now, most of the players who won the European championship for Germany in England last June earn their livings not just with Bayern but in Dortmund who pay the biggest salaries in the Bundesliga.

Historically Dortmund have a long way to go before they can match Bayern's record 13 league titles. The Ruhr club have just five championships to their name and their 1995 triumph was their first since 1963.
But in the mid-1990s when money, marketing and television deals are the key elements of running a successful football club, Dortmund are serious rivals to Bayern, the Bundesliga's richest club.

Dortmund can boast just 4,500 members compared to Bayern's 49,800. But trying to buy a ticket in Borussia's Westfalenstadium for any league match is as testing as finding a German town centre without a sausage stand.
Last season Dortmund boasted average crowds of 41,886, the second highest in the league behind Bayern's 59,766.
The club are using the cash they have earned from numerous appearances in Europe in recent seasons to expand the stadium.
Dortmund will fill the extra seats without trying. Despite the unemployment problems of the industrial Ruhr region, the club has fanatical supporters.
If Bayern is the jewel of Bavaria, Dortmund is the most precious stone in the Ruhr.
The club is run with marketing flair. Walk around any shopping centre in Germany and there will be a 12-year-old wearing a bright yellow Borussia shirt.
Dortmund is all about solid sponsoring deals, marketing, guaranteed capacity crowds and lucrative appearances in Europe.

Just a few years ago it would have been unthinkable that the club could have attracted Germany's big names to one of the most unattractive parts of the country. Until the 1990s Dortmund was a pretty average club.

Yet in recent years it frustrated Bayern by buying up major internationals like libero Sammer, playmaker Moeller, wing-back Stefan Reuter and defender Juergen Kohler when they returned from periods in Italy.
Bayern have the tradition and more money behind them and a chairman called Franz Beckenbauer. But Dortmund can beat them to a player's signature.

The fact is that the Bavarians have won the title just twice in the 1990s. Beckenbauer can only look with envy at Dortmund's lucrative appearances in the champions' league after his club crashed out of the UEFA Cup in the first round this year.
